class simulusion.world_model.dreamer.DreamerWorldModel(model)[source]#

Bases: WorldModelBase

The RSSM of a Dreamer agent, with its decoder, reward and discount heads.

encode filters the context through the posterior, step samples the prior, exactly as DreamerStepper does (and so as Dreamer’s own imagination does). Actions are continuous in [-1, 1]. terminated is the discount head’s continue probability falling below 0.5; models trained without that head have none.

Parameters:

model (Any) – A Dreamer, DreamerV2 or the DreamerAgent wrapping one.

family: ClassVar[str] = 'dreamer'#

Registry key, also written to the manifest.

PlaNet as a WorldModel.

class simulusion.world_model.planet.PlanetWorldModel(model, *, bit_depth=None)[source]#

Bases: WorldModelBase

PlaNet’s recurrent state-space model.

encode filters the context with the posterior mean, the way PlaNet’s CEM planner (RSSMPolicy) tracks the real episode; step advances the deterministic state and samples the prior, as the planner’s candidate rollouts do. Frames are quantised to bit_depth bits first, matching PlaNet’s preprocessing without its training-time dequantisation noise. PlaNet has a reward head but no termination head; its continuous actions are unbounded.

Parameters:

  • model (Any) – A Planet or its RecurrentStateSpaceModel.

  • bit_depth (Optional[int]) – Bits per colour channel the model was trained on (PlaNet’s default is 5).

family: ClassVar[str] = 'planet'#

Registry key, also written to the manifest.

IRIS as a WorldModel.

class simulusion.world_model.iris.IRISTokenWorldModel(agent, *, temperature=1.0, sample=True)[source]#

Bases: WorldModelBase

IRIS’s discrete autoencoder and Transformer, one frame at a time.

The state is the token history: tokens (B, T, K) for the last T frames and actions (B, T - 1) between them. step primes a fresh key/value cache with that history, then generates the next frame’s K tokens and reads the reward and termination heads at the action position, through the same Transformer calls imagine_rollout() makes. The history keeps at most WorldModelSpec.max_context frames, the window imagine_rollout falls back to when its cache fills up.

Rewards come out on the scale IRIS was trained on (sign-transformed by default, see IRISConfig.reward_transform).

The agent is switched to eval mode: its quantizer revives dead codes in training mode, which would rewrite the codebook on every call.

Parameters:

  • agent (Any) – An IRISAgent.

  • temperature (float) – Softmax temperature for sampling next-frame tokens.

  • sample (bool) – Sample tokens (default, as IRIS imagines); False takes the most likely token, which makes step deterministic.

family: ClassVar[str] = 'iris'#

Registry key, also written to the manifest.

class simulusion.world_model.diamond.DiamondWorldModel(model, *, sampling_steps=None)[source]#

Bases: WorldModelBase

DIAMOND’s diffusion model and reward/termination model.

Each frame is sampled by the diffusion model conditioned on the last L = num_conditioning_frames frames and the actions taken at them, exactly as in DIAMOND’s imagination: the reward/termination model scores (x_i, a_i), then the sampler draws x_{i+1}. encode needs L frames; without actions the context is taken to have been reached with action 0 (NOOP in Atari). Rewards are DIAMOND’s clipped classes {-1, 0, 1}.

Parameters:

  • model (Any) – A DiamondAgent, or any object with its config, diffusion_model, sampler and reward_model (None for a model trained without one).

  • sampling_steps (Optional[int]) – Override the Euler denoising steps per frame. Fewer is faster and blurrier; the paper uses 3.

family: ClassVar[str] = 'diamond'#

Registry key, also written to the manifest.

Genie as a WorldModel.

class simulusion.world_model.genie.GenieWorldModel(model, *, temperature=None)[source]#

Bases: WorldModelBase

Genie: video tokens in, latent actions drive the next frame.

Genie learns its actions from unlabelled video, so the action space is action_vocab_size latent actions (spec.action.latent is set): what each one does is whatever the model discovered. Without actions, encode labels the context’s transitions with the actions Genie infers itself. Genie has no reward or termination head.

The dynamics model sees at most num_frames frames, so the state keeps a rolling window of that many: tokens (B, T, N) and actions (B, T - 1). decode decodes the whole window, because the tokenizer’s decoder attends over time, and returns its last frame.

Parameters:

  • model (Any) – A Genie.

  • temperature (Optional[float]) – Sampling temperature for next-frame tokens. None keeps the model’s (2.0 in the paper); 0 takes the most likely token.

family: ClassVar[str] = 'genie'#

Registry key, also written to the manifest.

Ha & Schmidhuber’s World Models (ConvVAE + MDN-RNN) as a WorldModel.

class simulusion.world_model.vae_mdrnn.MDRNNWorldModel(vae, mdrnn, *, temperature=1.0)[source]#

Bases: WorldModelBase

A ConvVAE for pixels and an MDN-RNN for dynamics (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018).

encode maps each frame to its VAE latent mean and runs the MDN-RNN’s LSTM over the context. step predicts a Gaussian mixture over the next latent and samples it, at temperature as in the paper: the mixture weights are sharpened or flattened by it and the standard deviations scaled by its square root. The reward and done heads give reward and terminated (done logit above 0). Actions are continuous and unbounded.

Parameters:

  • vae (Any) – The ConvVAE.

  • mdrnn (Any) – The MDN-RNN, as trained (MDRNN) or as a single-step MDRNNCell.

  • temperature (float) – Sampling temperature tau; 0 takes the mean of the most likely mixture component.

family: ClassVar[str] = 'world-models'#

Registry key, also written to the manifest.

Training#

The one training loop every Simulusion family runs on.

from simulusion.training import Trainer, TrainerConfig
from simulusion.training.tasks import GenieTask, GenieTaskConfig

result = Trainer(TrainerConfig(max_steps=10_000, precision="bf16")).fit(
    GenieTask(GenieTaskConfig(data=VideoDataConfig(path="data/clips")))
)
result.world_model_path  # runs/<name>/world_model, loadable with load_world_model

A run uses one device: a CPU, one GPU, or Apple MPS. Precision is a run setting (fp32, bf16, fp16, auto) applied through MixedPrecision, rather than a flag per model.

Every run gets a directory holding everything needed to reproduce it:

runs/<run_name>/
    config.yaml          # the fully resolved run config: re-run with --config
    run.json             # git commit, package versions, host, command line
    metrics.jsonl        # every logged metric
    checkpoints/step_000500/   # resumable: trainer.resume=<this dir> or "auto"
    world_model/         # the trained world model (WorldModel protocol)

  • log_every (int) – Log metrics every this many units of progress.

  • eval_every (int) – Evaluate every this many units; 0 only at the end.

  • checkpoint_every (int) – Checkpoint every this many units; 0 only at the end.

  • keep_checkpoints (int) – Periodic checkpoints kept on disk (oldest dropped). The final one is always kept.

  • run_name (str | None) – Run directory name; a timestamped one when None.

  • resume (str | None) – A checkpoint directory to resume from, or "auto" for the newest complete checkpoint of out_dir/run_name.

  • export_world_model (bool) – Write the task’s world model to <run>/world_model when training ends.

What a family plugs into the shared Trainer.

A TrainingTask is everything that differs between families: which networks and optimizers exist, where batches come from (a dataset, a replay buffer filled by an environment), and what one unit of training does. The trainer owns everything that does not differ: the device, precision, seeding, the step budget, logging, evaluation cadence, early stopping, checkpoints and resuming, and exporting the world model at the end.

@register_task("my-model")
class MyTask(TrainingTask):
    config_cls = MyTaskConfig        # dataclass; its fields are YAML sections

    def setup(self, trainer):
        self.model = trainer.prepare_module(MyModel(**...))
        self.update = trainer.gradient_update(
            torch.optim.Adam(self.model.parameters()), self.model.parameters()
        )
        self.batches = trainer.infinite(trainer.prepare_dataloader(loader))

    def train_step(self):
        with self.trainer.precision.autocast():
            loss = self.model(next(self.batches).to(self.trainer.device))
        self.update(loss)
        return {"loss": loss.item()}

A task is the “agent” half of a family: it may hold a world model and a policy and decide how they train together. The world model itself stays a separate object, reachable through TrainingTask.world_model(), so it can be saved, evaluated or planned with on its own.

Mixed precision and optimizer steps shared by every trainer.

Each family used to carry its own use_amp flag, a GradScaler("cuda") per optimizer and the same six lines around backward(). They live here once, so a run’s precision is one setting rather than a flag per model:

precision = MixedPrecision("bf16", device)
update = GradientUpdate(optimizer, model.parameters(), precision, max_grad_norm=1.0)

with precision.autocast():
    loss = model(batch)
grad_norm = update(loss)

GradientUpdate keeps a loss scaler per optimizer. Algorithms with several optimizers (a world model, an actor and a critic) step them one after another, and a scaler shared between them would let an overflow in one skip the others.

class simulusion.training.precision.GradientUpdate(optimizer, parameters, precision, *, max_grad_norm=None, accumulation_steps=1)[source]#

Bases: object

One optimizer’s step: zero, backward, unscale, clip, step.

Parameters:

  • optimizer (torch.optim.Optimizer) – The optimizer to step.

  • parameters (Iterable[torch.Tensor]) – The parameters to clip; normally the ones optimizer owns.

  • precision (MixedPrecision) – Decides whether the loss is scaled.

  • max_grad_norm (Optional[float]) – Clip threshold, or None not to clip. The norm is measured after unscaling, so the threshold means the same thing at every precision.

  • accumulation_steps (int) – Optimizer steps happen every this many calls; the calls in between only add gradients. Each loss is divided by it, so the step sees the mean over the accumulated batches.

Calling it returns the gradient norm before clipping (a tensor), or None on a call that only accumulated. A non-finite norm under fp16 means the scaler skipped the step.

Run any training task from one YAML file.

A run config names a task and fills its sections:

task: genie
trainer:            # TrainerConfig: budget, precision, logging, checkpoints
  max_steps: 20000
  precision: bf16
model:              # the family's own config (GenieConfig here)
  num_frames: 16
data:               # where batches come from
  path: data/clips

Train it from the command line, with key=value overrides for any field (nested keys use dots):

simulusion train --config genie.yaml trainer.max_steps=500 model.dynamics_depth=4
simulusion train genie data.path=data/clips          # defaults for the rest

or from Python with run(). Every run writes its fully resolved config to <run_dir>/config.yaml; passing that file back with --config repeats the run. Example configs for each task live in simulusion/configs/runs/.

simulusion.training.run.RUN_CONFIG_DIR = PosixPath('/home/runner/work/simulusion/simulusion/simulusion/configs/runs')#

Data#

The episode: Simulusion’s one trajectory format, for video and for RL.

An Episode with T frames has T - 1 transitions, the same convention as the WorldModel protocol: actions[t] is the action taken at frames[t], which led to frames[t + 1] and earned rewards[t]; terminated[t] says frames[t + 1] ended the episode, truncated[t] that it was cut off (a time limit) without ending. Everything but frames is optional, so a plain video is an episode too.

On disk an episode is one .npz file:

Key

Contents

Required

frames

(T, H, W, C) uint8, the main camera

yes

actions

(T-1,) int (discrete) or (T-1, A)

no

rewards

(T-1,) float

no

terminated

(T-1,) bool

no

truncated

(T-1,) bool

no

frames.<camera>

(T, H, W, C) uint8, further cameras

no

obs.<name>

(T, ...) low-dimensional observations (robot joint state, proprioception)

no

language

0-d string, a task instruction

no

This is the layout RecordingWrapper writes, extended for robot data (several cameras, proprioception, language).

Fixed-length windows over episodes, as a PyTorch dataset.

World models train on short clips cut from longer episodes. A SequenceDataset indexes every window of sequence_length frames that fits inside an episode and returns it as a dict of tensors:

Frames stay uint8 so batches are a quarter of the size on the way to the GPU; tasks convert them with frames_to_float().

Read LeRobot datasets as Simulusion episodes.

LeRobot is the Hugging Face format most open robot datasets now ship in. LeRobotEpisodes reads one from a local folder, without the lerobot package: the format is Parquet for the low-dimensional signals plus MP4 per camera, described by meta/info.json. Both layouts are supported:

  • v2.x: one Parquet file and one MP4 per camera per episode, listed in meta/episodes.jsonl.

  • v3.0: many episodes per Parquet / MP4 file, located through the meta/episodes/ tables (row ranges and video timestamps).

from simulusion.data import LeRobotEpisodes, SequenceDataset

episodes = LeRobotEpisodes("datasets/pusht")         # a local dataset folder
episodes[0].frames.shape                               # (T, 96, 96, 3)
episodes[0].actions.shape                              # (T - 1, 2)
windows = SequenceDataset(episodes, sequence_length=16)

or convert once to an episode folder: simulusion datasets import lerobot datasets/pusht data/pusht. Needs pip install simulusion[lerobot] (PyArrow and PyAV).

How LeRobot maps onto Episode: the chosen camera becomes frames and the others cameras; action becomes actions minus its last row (it leads past the final frame); next.reward and next.done become rewards and terminated the same way, with the final next.done moved onto the last transition; other numeric observation.* features become observations (so observation.state is observations["state"]); the episode’s first task becomes language.

Convert RLDS episodes into Simulusion episodes.

RLDS (the format of Open X-Embodiment and many other robot datasets) stores each episode as a sequence of steps, every step a dict with an observation (itself a dict of cameras and state), an action, a reward and the flags is_first / is_last / is_terminal.

episode_from_rlds() turns one such episode, given as plain Python and NumPy values, into an Episode; reading the dataset files themselves is left to whatever produced the steps.

RLDS puts the action in the step it is taken from, so a T-step episode has T actions; the last one leads past the final observation and is dropped, as are its reward and flags. is_terminal on the final step marks the last transition terminated; an episode that ends without it is truncated.

Agents#

Act through any world model by planning in it.

A WorldModel with a reward head is enough to choose actions: imagine many action sequences, score them by predicted return, keep the best. CEMPlanner does that with the cross-entropy method, the planner PlaNet uses, but through the shared protocol only, so it works on every family’s world model: one trained with its agent, or alone from a dataset (dreamer-wm, iris-wm, diamond-wm, mdrnn).

from simulusion.agents import CEMPlanner, PlanningAgent, run_episode
from simulusion.world_model import load_world_model

model = load_world_model("runs/dreamer-wm_.../world_model")
agent = PlanningAgent(model, CEMPlanner(horizon=12, candidates=500))
episode_return = run_episode(env, agent)
class simulusion.agents.planning.CEMPlanner(horizon=12, candidates=500, iterations=5, elites=50, discount=0.99, init_std=1.0, min_std=0.05, smoothing=0.0)[source]#

Bases: object

Cross-entropy-method planning over a world model’s imagined returns.

Each of iterations rounds samples candidates action sequences of length horizon, imagines them all in one batched rollout, and refits the sampling distribution to the elites with the highest discounted predicted return. Continuous actions are Gaussian (clipped to the action bounds); discrete ones are a categorical per step. Imagined returns stop accumulating once the model predicts the episode ended.

Variables:

  • horizon (int) – Steps per imagined sequence.

  • candidates (int) – Sequences per round.

  • iterations (int) – Refitting rounds.

  • elites (int) – Best sequences each refit uses.

  • discount (float) – Per-step discount of imagined rewards.

  • init_std (float) – Initial standard deviation of continuous actions.

  • min_std (float) – Floor on the refitted standard deviation.

  • smoothing (float) – Weight of the old distribution in each refit (0 = none).

Parameters:

  • horizon (int)

  • candidates (int)

  • iterations (int)

  • elites (int)

  • discount (float)

  • init_std (float)

  • min_std (float)

  • smoothing (float)

class simulusion.agents.planning.PlanningAgent(model, planner=None, *, context=None)[source]#

Bases: object

An agent that keeps recent frames and plans each action in the world model.

Every act() re-encodes the last context frames and the actions between them (the protocol’s encode()), then plans from that state. Recurrent models (Dreamer, PlaNet, V + M) carry the whole history in their state, so a short context is only an approximation for them; models with a fixed window (IRIS, DIAMOND, Genie) see exactly what they were trained to see.

Parameters:

  • model (WorldModel) – Any world model with a reward head.

  • planner (Optional[CEMPlanner]) – How actions are chosen; CEMPlanner by default.

  • context (Optional[int]) – Frames kept; the model’s max_context (or its context_frames when that is unbounded), at least 1.

Models sub-module - Core world model implementations.

Exported Components:
Agents (High-level training wrappers):

  • DreamerAgent: High-level Dreamer training API

  • JEPAAgent: JEPA agent for self-supervised learning

  • Planet: PlaNet planning agent

  • VisionTransformer: Vision Transformer for image encoding

  • ModularRSSM: Modular RSSM with swappable components

  • Genie: Generative Interactive Environment model

Core Models:

  • Dreamer: Core Dreamer implementation with RSSM, actor, critic

  • RSSM: Recurrent State-Space Model (Dreamer-style)

  • RecurrentStateSpaceModel: PlaNet-style RSSM

  • LatentActionModel: Latent action learning for Genie

  • DynamicsModel: Future frame prediction for Genie

Factory Functions:

  • create_genie, create_genie_small, create_genie_large

  • create_modular_rssm

  • create_latent_action_model, create_dynamics_model

class simulusion.models.dreamer_rssm.RSSM(action_size, stoch_size, deter_size, hidden_size, obs_embed_size, activation)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Recurrent State-Space Model used by Dreamer for latent dynamics learning.

The RSSM is the core world model component that learns compact representations of environment dynamics. It maintains a hybrid state consisting of:

  1. Deterministic State (h) – A recurrent hidden state updated by a GRU, capturing sequential/temporal information and deterministic transitions.

  2. Stochastic State (s) – A latent variable representing stochastic, multi-modal uncertainty in the environment (e.g., ambiguous observations).

The model operates in two modes:

  • Observe Mode – Updates states using actual observations from the environment. Uses the representation model: p(s_t | h_t, obs_t)

  • Imagine Mode – Predicts future states without observations. Uses the transition/prior model: p(s_t | h_t)

Architecture

  • Input: Previous state (h_{t-1}, s_{t-1}) and action a_{t-1}

  • Process: GRU updates deterministic state, MLP computes stochastic prior/posterior

  • Output: Updated state (h_t, s_t) and distributions

State Representation

  • deter (h): GRU hidden state, captures sequential context

  • stoch (s): Stochastic latent, multi-modal uncertainty

  • mean/std: Parameters of the stochastic distribution

Usage with DreamerAgent:

rssm = RSSM(
    action_size=action_dim,
    stoch_size=30,      # Stochastic state dimension
    deter_size=200,     # Deterministic (GRU) state dimension
    hidden_size=200,    # MLP hidden layer size
    obs_embed_size=256,  # Observation embedding from encoder
    activation='elu'
)

# Observe with actual observation
posterior, prior = rssm.observe_step(prev_state, prev_action, obs_embed)

# Imagine future without observation
prior = rssm.imagine_step(current_state, action)

Training

The RSSM is trained by maximizing the ELBO (Evidence Lower Bound):

  • KL divergence between prior and posterior encourages the prior to capture environment dynamics

  • Reconstruction loss from decoder ensures state captures observation info

Reference:

Dreamer: Scalable Reinforcement Learning Using World Models Hafner et al., 2020 - https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01603

Parameters:

  • action_size (int)

  • stoch_size (int)

  • deter_size (int)

  • hidden_size (int)

  • obs_embed_size (int)

  • activation (str)

observe_step(prev_state, prev_action, obs_embed, nonterm=tensor(1.), noise=None)[source]#

Update state using actual observation (observe mode).

In observe mode, the RSSM first computes a transition prior from the previous state and action, then refines the stochastic state using the actual observation embedding to form the posterior.

Parameters:

  • prev_state (dict) – Dictionary with ‘deter’ (h_{t-1}) and ‘stoch’ (s_{t-1})

  • prev_action (Tensor) – Previous action a_{t-1}, shape (B, action_size)

  • obs_embed (Tensor) – Observation embedding from encoder, shape (B, obs_embed_size)

  • nonterm (Tensor) – Termination mask (1.0 = continue, 0.0 = terminal)

  • noise (Tuple[Tensor, Tensor] | None) – Optional (prior_noise, posterior_noise) standard-normal tensors of shape (B, stoch_size) used for the two samples instead of drawing them internally. Passing noise makes the step a pure function of its inputs, which exported graphs and eager-vs-exported parity checks need.

Returns:

A tuple (posterior, prior) of state dictionaries. The posterior incorporates observation information; the prior is the transition prediction before observation. Both share the same deterministic state because the GRU is only advanced once per timestep.

The order differs from observe_rollout() and from ModularRSSM.observe_step, which both return (prior, posterior). The dictionaries have identical keys, so a swapped unpacking fails silently: acting on the prior discards the current observation. It is kept for backward compatibility.

Return type:

Tuple[dict, dict]

imagine_step(prev_state, prev_action, nonterm=tensor(1.), noise=None)[source]#

Predict next state without observation (imagine mode).

In imagine mode, the RSSM predicts future states using only the prior distribution. This is used for planning and policy learning where actual observations are not available.

Parameters:

  • prev_state (dict) – Dictionary with ‘deter’ (h_{t-1}) and ‘stoch’ (s_{t-1})

  • prev_action (Tensor) – Previous action a_{t-1}, shape (B, action_size)

  • nonterm (Tensor) – Termination mask (1.0 = continue, 0.0 = terminal)

  • noise (Tensor | None) – Optional standard-normal tensor (B, stoch_size) used for the stochastic sample instead of drawing one internally.

Returns:

  • deter: Predicted deterministic state

  • mean, std, stoch: Prior stochastic state distribution

Return type:

Dictionary with predicted state containing

observe_rollout(obs_embed, actions, nonterms, init_state, seq_len)[source]#

Process a sequence of observations (observe mode rollout).

At each timestep we run observe_step once to obtain the transition prior (the prediction given the previous state and action) and the observation-informed posterior. The posterior is then used as the previous state for the next step, matching the standard Dreamer inference pattern.

Parameters:

  • obs_embed (Tensor) – Observation embeddings, shape (T+1, B, obs_embed_size)

  • actions (Tensor) – Actions, shape (T, B, action_size)

  • nonterms (Tensor) – Non-termination flags, shape (T, B, 1)

  • init_state (dict) – Initial state dictionary

  • seq_len (int) – Sequence length T

Returns:

Dictionary with prior states stacked along the time axis posterior: Dictionary with posterior states stacked along the time axis

Return type:

prior

Mixture Density Recurrent Neural Network (MDRNN) model implementation.

This module provides implementations of MDRNN models for world modeling. The MDRNN is used to predict future latent states given current latent states and actions, using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) for the output.

Reference:

Ha & Schmidhuber (2018). Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11111

class simulusion.models.mdrnn.MDRNN(latents, actions, hiddens, gaussians)[source]#

Bases: _MDRNNBase

MDRNN model for multi-step sequence prediction.

This model processes entire sequences of latent states and actions, predicting the next latent state using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). It also predicts rewards and terminal states.

Parameters:

  • latents (int) – Dimensionality of latent space (input and output).

  • actions (int) – Dimensionality of action space.

  • hiddens (int) – Number of hidden units in LSTM.

  • gaussians (int) – Number of Gaussian components in GMM output.

Example

>>> mdrnn = MDRNN(latents=32, actions=3, hiddens=256, gaussians=5)
>>> actions = torch.randn(10, 4, 3)  # seq_len, batch, action
>>> latents = torch.randn(10, 4, 32)  # seq_len, batch, latent
>>> mus, sigmas, logpi, rs, ds = mdrnn(actions, latents)
>>> # mus.shape = (10, 4, 5, 32)
forward(actions, latents)[source]#

Multi-step forward pass through the MDRNN.

Parameters:

  • actions (Tensor) – (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE, ASIZE) Tensor of actions.

  • latents (Tensor) – (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE, LSIZE) Tensor of latent states.

Returns:

  • mus: (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE, N_GAUSS, LSIZE) GMM means

  • sigmas: (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE, N_GAUSS, LSIZE) GMM standard deviations

  • logpi: (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE, N_GAUSS) log GMM weights

  • rs: (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE) predicted rewards

  • ds: (SEQ_LEN, BSIZE) predicted terminal state logits

Return type:

Tuple of

class simulusion.models.mdrnn.MDRNNCell(latents, actions, hiddens, gaussians)[source]#

Bases: _MDRNNBase

MDRNN model for single-step forward prediction.

This model processes a single step of latent state and action,

This model processes a single step of latent state and action, predicting the next latent state using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM). It also predicts rewards and terminal states. Useful for real-time inference.

Parameters:

  • latents (int) – Dimensionality of latent space (input and output).

  • actions (int) – Dimensionality of action space.

  • hiddens (int) – Number of hidden units in LSTMCell.

  • gaussians (int) – Number of Gaussian components in GMM output.

Example

>>> cell = MDRNNCell(latents=32, actions=3, hiddens=256, gaussians=5)
>>> action = torch.randn(4, 3)  # batch, action
>>> latent = torch.randn(4, 32)  # batch, latent
>>> hidden = (torch.randn(4, 256), torch.randn(4, 256))
>>> mus, sigmas, logpi, r, d, next_hidden = cell(action, latent, hidden)

Linear Controller for World Models.

This module provides a simple linear controller that maps latent states and recurrent hidden states to actions. The controller is trained using CMA-ES (Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy).

Reference:

Ha & Schmidhuber (2018). Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11111

class simulusion.models.controller.Controller(latent_size, hidden_size, action_size)[source]#

Bases: Module

Linear controller that maps latent + hidden state to actions.

This is a simple linear controller that takes the latent state and recurrent hidden state as input and outputs actions. It is trained separately from the world model using black-box optimization (CMA-ES).

Variables:

  • latent_size – Dimensionality of latent state from VAE.

  • hidden_size – Dimensionality of RSSM hidden state.

  • action_size – Dimensionality of action space.

Parameters:

  • latent_size (int)

  • hidden_size (int)

  • action_size (int)

Example

>>> controller = Controller(latent_size=32, hidden_size=200, action_size=3)
>>> state = torch.cat([latent, hidden], dim=-1)
>>> action = controller(state)
forward(state)[source]#

class simulusion.models.modular_rssm.ModularRSSM(encoder, decoder, backbone, reward_decoder=None)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Modular RSSM with swappable encoder, decoder, and backbone.

This class allows researchers to easily experiment with different: - Encoders: Conv, MLP, ViT - Decoders: Conv, MLP - Backbones: GRU, LSTM, Transformer

Example

>>> encoder = ConvEncoder((3, 64, 64), embed_size=1024)
>>> decoder = ConvDecoder(32, 200, (3, 64, 64))
>>> backbone = GRUBackbone(action_size=6, stoch_size=32, deter_size=200, hidden_size=200, embed_size=1024)
>>> rssm = ModularRSSM(encoder, decoder, backbone)
Parameters:

  • encoder (EncoderBase)

  • decoder (DecoderBase)

  • backbone (BackboneBase)

  • reward_decoder (DecoderBase | None)

act(frame, epsilon=0.0, temperature=1.0, hidden=None, return_hidden=False)[source]#

Sample action from policy.

The policy is recurrent (paper A.3: CNN -> LSTM). Callers stepping an episode must thread hidden from one call to the next and reset it on episode boundaries; dropping it makes the policy effectively memoryless, which for games like Pong removes any way to infer the ball’s direction from a single frame.

Parameters:

  • frame (Tensor) – Single frame (B, C, H, W)

  • epsilon (float) – Random action probability

  • temperature (float) – Action distribution temperature

  • hidden (Tuple[Tensor, Tensor] | None) – LSTM state from the previous step, or None to start fresh

  • return_hidden (bool) – If True, also return the updated LSTM state

Returns:

Selected actions (B,), and the updated LSTM state when return_hidden is set.

Return type:

actions

burn_in(frames)[source]#

Initialise the LSTM state by replaying preceding frames.

Paper A.3: “Before starting the imagination procedure from a given frame, we burn-in the 20 previous frames to initialize the hidden state” (Kapturowski et al., 2019). Without this the rollout begins from a zero state that the policy never sees at collection time.

Parameters:

frames (Tensor) – Preceding observations (B, T_burn, C, H, W), already in the reconstruction domain the policy is trained on.

Returns:

The LSTM state after the burn-in, or None if no frames were given.

Return type:

Tuple[Tensor, Tensor] | None

transform_reward(rewards)[source]#

Apply the configured reward transform.

Atari rewards are unbounded integers – in the thousands for games like Krull or UpNDown – and feeding them raw into the value function and lambda-return makes the critic’s target scale game-dependent. The standard Atari convention, which IRIS follows, is to take the sign.

Parameters:

rewards (Tensor)

Return type:

Tensor

reconstruct(frames)[source]#

Pass frames through the discrete autoencoder: D(E(x)).

Paper A.1: “during experience collection in the real environment, frames still go through the autoencoder to keep the input distribution of the policy unchanged”. The policy only ever learns from reconstructions during imagination, so feeding it raw frames in the real environment is a distribution shift.

The encoder is forced into eval mode for the duration. This is not cosmetic: the quantizer’s dead-code revival only runs in training mode, and this method is called on single frames during experience collection and evaluation, when the agent is still in training mode. Leaving it there re-seeds most of the codebook from the 16 encoder outputs of one frame on every environment step, destroying the vocabulary the world model is being trained against.

Parameters:

frames (Tensor) – Real observations (B, C, H, W) or (B, T, C, H, W) in [0, 1].

Returns:

Reconstructions with the same shape, clamped to [0, 1].

Return type:

Tensor

imagine_rollout(initial_frame, horizon=20, burn_in_frames=None, sample_tokens=True, temperature=1.0, stop_on_termination=True)[source]#

Generate imagined trajectories using the world model.

Implements the imagination MDP of paper 2.3 / Figure 1: starting from a real observation, the policy acts on decoded frames while the Transformer rolls the dynamics forward, conditioned on the full imagined history.

Parameters:

  • initial_frame (Tensor) – Starting frame x_0 (B, C, H, W), in [0, 1].

  • horizon (int) – Number of steps H to imagine.

  • burn_in_frames (Tensor | None) – The (B, T_burn, C, H, W) reconstructed observations preceding initial_frame, used to initialise the policy’s LSTM state (paper A.3). None starts from a zero state.

  • sample_tokens (bool) – Sample next-frame tokens instead of taking the argmax.

  • temperature (float) – Sampling temperature for token generation.

  • stop_on_termination (bool) – Cut the rollout short once every trajectory in the batch has hit a predicted episode end (paper 2.3). Set False to always return exactly horizon steps; correctness does not depend on it, since continues already zeroes the discount past a termination.

Returns:

dict with frames (B, T+1, C, H, W), actions (B, T), rewards (B, T) and continues (B, T). T may be shorter than horizon if every rollout predicted an episode end.

Return type:

trajectory

class simulusion.models.iris_transformer.KVCache(num_layers, batch_size, num_heads, head_dim, max_len, device, dtype)[source]#

Bases: object

Per-layer key/value cache for incremental decoding.

Imagination generates one position at a time. Without a cache, producing the K tokens of a frame means re-running the whole Transformer over the entire prefix K times, which is O(K * L^2) per imagined step. Caching the keys and values of every position already processed reduces that to O(K * L).

Storage is a pre-allocated (B, num_heads, max_len, head_dim) buffer per layer, filled left to right; length marks the valid prefix.

Parameters:

  • num_layers (int)

  • batch_size (int)

  • num_heads (int)

  • head_dim (int)

  • max_len (int)

  • device (device)

  • dtype (dtype)

append(layer, k, v)[source]#

Append this step’s keys/values for layer and return the full prefix.

The write offset is self.length, which the caller advances once per forward pass (after all layers have been visited), so every layer writes to the same slice.

Parameters:

  • layer (int)

  • k (Tensor)

  • v (Tensor)

Return type:

Tuple[Tensor, Tensor]

advance(steps)[source]#

Commit steps newly written positions.

Parameters:

steps (int)

Return type:

None

reset()[source]#

Empty the cache while keeping its buffers.

Re-priming a reset cache gives the same result as priming a fresh one: positions past length are never read. Reusing the buffers keeps a GraphedDecodeStep captured against them valid.

Return type:

None

class simulusion.models.iris_transformer.GraphedDecodeStep(model, cache, batch_size)[source]#

Bases: object

One single-position forward against a KVCache, as a CUDA graph.

Imagination decodes one position at a time, and each forward is about 160 small kernels. On a laptop GPU the CPU cost of launching them outweighs the GPU work several times over. Capturing the step once and replaying it launches it as one graph.

A graph needs fixed shapes, so instead of slicing the cache to its current length the step writes the new key/value at a position tensor and attends over the whole buffer with a mask hiding positions after it. Masked positions contribute exactly zero weight, so this computes the same function as IRISTransformer._forward_positions() for one position (inference only: dropout is not applied).

Capture writes to position 0 of cache, so build the step before priming the cache, and keep the same cache afterwards (KVCache.reset() instead of a new cache) so the captured buffers stay the ones in use.

Parameters:

  • model (IRISTransformer)

  • cache (KVCache)

  • batch_size (int)

class simulusion.models.iris_transformer.IRISTransformer(vocab_size=512, tokens_per_frame=16, action_size=18, embed_dim=256, num_layers=10, num_heads=4, dropout=0.1, gradient_checkpointing=False, reward_classes=3)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

GPT-like autoregressive Transformer for world modeling.

Models the dynamics of the environment by predicting, autoregressively over an interleaved sequence of frame tokens and actions:

  • Next frame tokens (transition model), one token at a time

  • Rewards

  • Episode termination

The sequence layout for S frames and S - 1 actions is:

z_0^1 ... z_0^K, a_0, z_1^1 ... z_1^K, a_1, ..., z_{S-2}^1 ... z_{S-2}^K,
a_{S-2}, z_{S-1}^1 ... z_{S-1}^K

A causal (lower-triangular) attention mask is always applied, so every position only attends to itself and preceding positions. The tokens of frame t + 1 are predicted starting from the action position a_t (which sees the whole of frame t and the action), then autoregressively from each previously predicted token of frame t + 1. This matches the paper’s

z_{t+1}^k ~ p(. | z_{<=t}, a_{<=t}, z_{t+1}^{<k})

Parameters:

  • vocab_size (int)

  • tokens_per_frame (int)

  • action_size (int)

  • embed_dim (int)

  • num_layers (int)

  • num_heads (int)

  • dropout (float)

  • gradient_checkpointing (bool)

  • reward_classes (int)

prime_cache(tokens, actions, cache, start_pos=0)[source]#

Fill a cache with an interleaved (frame, action) history in one pass.

This is the “conditioning” phase of imagination: the real frames (and the actions taken between them) are pushed through the model so that subsequent single-position steps attend to the full history, exactly as the teacher-forced training sequence does.

  • actions (Tensor | None) – Actions following each frame. Pass Tc actions to end the primed sequence on an action (ready to generate the next frame), or Tc - 1 / None to end on the last frame’s tokens.

  • cache (KVCache) – Cache to fill; must be empty or positioned at start_pos.

  • start_pos (int) – Absolute position of the first embedded token.

Returns:

The absolute position just past the primed sequence.

Return type:

int

Generate one frame’s K tokens incrementally, one position at a time.

The cache must already hold the history up to and including the current frame’s tokens. class simulusion.models.genie.Genie(num_frames=16, image_size=64, in_channels=3, tokenizer_vocab_size=1024, tokenizer_embedding_dim=32, tokenizer_encoder_dim=512, tokenizer_decoder_dim=1024, action_vocab_size=8, action_embedding_dim=32, action_encoder_dim=1024, action_decoder_dim=1024, dynamics_dim=5120, dynamics_depth=48, dynamics_num_heads=40, encoder_depth=12, decoder_depth=20, latent_action_depth=20, use_bfloat16=False, action_pooling='mean', window_attention_heads=1, tokenizer_num_heads=16, action_num_heads=16)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Genie: Generative Interactive Environment.

A generative model trained from video-only data that can be used as an interactive environment. Contains three key components: 1. Video Tokenizer: Converts raw video frames into discrete tokens 2. Latent Action Model (LAM): Infers latent actions between frames 3. Dynamics Model: Predicts future frames given past frames and latent actions

Based on “Genie: Generative Interactive Environments” paper (arXiv:2402.15391).

Training follows two phases as per paper: 1. Train video tokenizer first (on video tokens) 2. Co-train LAM (from pixels) and dynamics model (on video tokens)

The LAM uses VQ-VAE training with: - Encoder: Takes x1:t and x_{t+1} → outputs latent actions - Decoder: Takes x1:t-1 (masked) + actions → reconstructs x_t - Auxiliary variance loss to prevent action collapse

At inference, latent actions are stopgrad’d when passed to dynamics model.

Parameters:

  • num_frames (int)

  • image_size (int)

  • in_channels (int)

  • tokenizer_vocab_size (int)

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Latent Action Model (LAM) for unsupervised action learning.

Learns discrete latent actions from unlabeled video frames using a VQ-VAE based objective. The model infers latent actions between frames that encode the most meaningful changes for future frame prediction.

Based on Genie paper - learns actions without action labels from Internet videos.

Components: - Encoder: Takes all previous frames x1:t and next frame x_t+1 → outputs latent actions - Decoder: Takes previous frames x1:t-1 and latent actions a1:t-1 → predicts next frame x_t

simulusion.models.diffusion.DiT.sinusoidal_time_embedding(timesteps, dim, max_period=10000.0)[source]#

Create sinusoidal timestep embeddings for diffusion conditioning.

Math:

embedding[t] = [sin(t / P^(2i/d)), cos(t / P^(2i/d))] for i in [0, d/2)

Note the division by increasing powers of max_period: frequencies decay from 1 down to 1/max_period. Building them the other way round (ascending to max_period) makes the sine argument reach ~1e7 radians at t=999, which aliases so badly that adjacent timesteps receive near-orthogonal embeddings – the model then has to memorise every noise level instead of interpolating between them.

Parameters:

  • timesteps (Tensor) – Tensor of timesteps, shape (B,) or (B, 1)

  • dim (int) – Embedding dimension

  • max_period (float) – Longest sinusoid period; 10000 follows DDPM/ADM.

Returns:

Tensor of shape (B, dim) with sinusoidal embeddings.

Return type:

Tensor

simulusion.models.diffusion.DiT.get_2d_sincos_pos_embed(embed_dim, grid_size)[source]#

Fixed 2D sine-cosine positional embeddings (ViT/DiT convention).

The paper applies “standard ViT frequency-based positional embeddings (the sine-cosine version) to all input tokens” after patchify. These are constant, not learned, which is what lets a trained model be evaluated at a different token count without the embeddings being meaningless.

Parameters:

  • grid_size (int) – Tokens per side, i.e. input_size // patch_size.

Returns:

class simulusion.models.diffusion.DiT.PatchEmbed(img_size, patch_size, in_channels, embed_dim, learnable_pos=False)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Patchify an image into a sequence of learnable patch tokens.

Used in Vision Transformers (ViT) and DiT to convert 2D images into sequences of token embeddings that can be processed by transformers.

Process:

  1. Conv2d with kernel_size=stride=patch_size extracts non-overlapping patches

  2. Each patch is projected to embed_dim via linear layer (Conv2d)

  3. Learnable positional embeddings are added for spatial information

Input: (B, C, H, W) images Output: (B, N, embed_dim) where N = (H/patch_size) * (W/patch_size)

Parameters:

  • img_size (int) – Image size (assumes square), e.g., 32 for CIFAR

  • patch_size (int) – Size of each patch (typically 4, 8, or 16)

  • in_channels (int) – Number of input channels (3 for RGB)

  • embed_dim (int) – Output dimension for each patch token

  • learnable_pos (bool)

Usage with DiT:

patch_embed = PatchEmbed(img_size=32, patch_size=4, in_channels=3, embed_dim=256) tokens = patch_embed(images) # (B, 64, 256) for 32x32 image with patch_size=4

class simulusion.models.diffusion.DiT.TransformerBlock(d_model, n_heads, mlp_ratio, drop, t_dim=None)[source]#

Bases: Module

DiT block with adaLN-Zero conditioning (paper 3.2).

The conditioning vector – the sum of the timestep and class embeddings – is mapped by a single SiLU + Linear to six vectors per block: shift, scale and gate for each of the attention and MLP sub-layers. That is the 6x hidden output the paper specifies for adaLN-Zero (vanilla adaLN uses 4x because it has no gates).

The “-Zero” is the important half. The modulation layer is zero-initialised, so at step 0 every gate is 0 and the whole block is the identity function. Figure 5 shows this matters a lot: adaLN-Zero reaches roughly half the FID of in-context conditioning at 400K steps, and clearly beats vanilla adaLN, which is identical apart from the gates and their initialisation.

Normalisation is LayerNorm without affine parameters – the scale and shift come from the conditioning instead, so learned per-channel affines would be redundant.

Parameters:

  • d_model (int)

  • n_heads (int)

  • mlp_ratio (float)

  • drop (float)

  • t_dim (int | None)

forward(x, c)[source]#

Tensor

class simulusion.models.diffusion.diamond_diffusion.TimestepEmbedding(dim, freq_dim=256, max_period=10000.0)[source]#

Bases: Module

Sinusoidal noise-level embedding followed by an MLP.

The input is EDM’s c_noise = log(sigma) / 4 (Appendix C, eq. 11), which ranges over several units either side of zero as sigma sweeps the schedule. A plain Linear(1, ...) on that scalar – the previous implementation, despite the docstring – gives the network a single monotone feature to condition on, so nearby noise levels are nearly indistinguishable after the first layer. The sinusoidal expansion used by every U-Net in this lineage spreads the scalar across freq_dim frequencies first, which is what makes the noise level a usable conditioning signal.

Parameters:

  • dim (int)

  • freq_dim (int)

  • max_period (float)

class simulusion.models.diffusion.reward_termination.ResidualBlock(in_channels, out_channels, cond_dim=None)[source]#

Bases: Module

Residual block following DIAMOND Appendix D.

The main path is GroupNorm -> SiLU -> 3x3 convolution (stride 1, padding 1), added to a (optionally projected) skip connection. When cond_dim is provided the group normalization is made adaptive, i.e. its scale/shift are predicted from a conditioning vector (the action embedding) as used by the reward/termination model. The actor-critic omits conditioning and uses a plain group normalization.

  • out_channels (int)

Vision, tokenization, and layers#

Key classes: ConvEncoder, ConvDecoder, DenseDecoder, ActionDecoder, CNNEncoder, CNNDecoder, IRISEncoder, IRISDecoder, DiscreteAutoencoder, VectorQuantizer, VectorQuantizerEMA, VideoTokenizer, MultiHeadSelfAttention, and STTransformer.

Convolutional Variational Autoencoder (ConvVAE) implementation.

This module provides the ConvVAE model architecture for encoding and decoding images in the World Models framework. The VAE uses a convolutional encoder and decoder with a variational latent space.

class simulusion.vision.dreamer_encoder.ConvEncoder(input_shape, embed_size, activation, depth=32)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Convolutional observation encoder used by Dreamer world models.

This encoder transforms raw image observations (typically RGB frames from environments like Atari or DeepMind Control) into compact latent embeddings that can be processed by the RSSM (Recurrent State-Space Model).

  • Input: (B, C, H, W) raw images, values in [-0.5, 0.5]

  • Process: 4 convolutional layers with stride 2, halving spatial dimensions

  • Output: (B, embed_size) compact representation

The encoder uses a depth doubling pattern: 32 -> 64 -> 128 -> 256 channels. After convolutions, a fully connected layer projects from 1024 features to the desired embedding size.

Usage with Dreamer:

encoder = ConvEncoder(
    input_shape=(3, 64, 64),  # RGB 64x64 images
    embed_size=256,           # RSSM observation embedding size
    activation='relu'         # Activation function
)
obs_embedding = encoder(observation)  # (B, 256)
Parameters:

  • input_shape (tuple) – Tuple (C, H, W) for input images, typically (3, 64, 64)

  • embed_size (int) – Output embedding dimension, typically 256 or 1024

  • activation (str) – Activation function name (‘relu’, ‘elu’, ‘tanh’, etc.)

  • depth (int) – Base channel depth for first layer (default 32)

forward(inputs)[source]#
Parameters:

inputs (Tensor)

Return type:

Tensor

class simulusion.vision.dreamer_decoder.TanhBijector[source]#

Bases: Transform

Bijective tanh transform for squashing Gaussian distributions to [-1, 1].

This transformation is essential for Dreamer’s action policy. Raw neural network outputs are Gaussian distributions over R^n, but actions in continuous control environments are typically bounded in [-1, 1]. The tanh bijector provides:

  1. Bijective mapping: tanh is invertible (with atanh as inverse)

  2. Stable log-det Jacobian: Computable for gradient-based training

  3. Clipped actions: During inference, actions are naturally bounded

  • Forward: y = tanh(x)

  • Inverse: x = atanh(y) = 0.5 * log((1+y)/(1-y))

  • Log-det: log|dy/dx| = 2*(log(2) - x - softplus(-2x))

Usage with Dreamer ActionDecoder:

dist = TransformedDistribution(
    Normal(mean, std),
    TanhBijector()
)
action = dist.sample()  # Bounded to [-1, 1]
Reference:

Building a Scalable Deep RL Library by Learning from Mistakes, Haarnoja et al.

property sign: int#

Parameters:

x (Tensor)

Return type:

Tensor

class simulusion.vision.dreamer_decoder.ConvDecoder(stoch_size, deter_size, output_shape, activation, depth=32)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Convolutional decoder for reconstructing observations from latent states.

Part of Dreamer’s world model, this decoder reconstructs image observations from the combined stochastic (s) and deterministic (h) RSSM states.

  • Input: Concatenated [stoch_state, deter_state], shape (B, stoch+deter)

  • Process: Dense projection + 4 transposed convolutions (upsampling 2x each)

  • Output: Independent Normal distribution over observation pixels

The decoder mirrors the ConvEncoder’s structure but in reverse (transposed convs instead of regular convs). This creates a symmetric autoencoder where the encoder and decoder can be trained jointly to learn compressed representations.

Returns torch.distributions.Independent(Normal(mean, std), len(shape)) allowing log_prob(observation) computation for reconstruction loss.

Usage in Dreamer world model:

decoder = ConvDecoder(
    stoch_size=30,
    deter_size=200,
    output_shape=(3, 64, 64),  # RGB images
    activation='relu'
)
obs_dist = decoder(latent_features)  # Returns distribution
log_prob = obs_dist.log_prob(target_observation)

The reconstruction loss is -log_prob(observation), which encourages the RSSM to learn states that capture observation information.

Parameters:

  • stoch_size (int)

  • deter_size (int)

  • output_shape (tuple[int, ...])

  • activation (str)

  • depth (int)

forward(features)[source]#
Parameters:

features (Tensor)

Return type:

Independent

class simulusion.vision.dreamer_decoder.DenseDecoder(stoch_size, deter_size, output_shape, n_layers, units, activation, dist, num_buckets=255, symlog_range=10.0)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

MLP decoder for reward/value/discount prediction from latent features.

Part of Dreamer’s world model, this decoder predicts scalar quantities (rewards, values, discount factors) from RSSM latent states.

  • Input: [stoch_state, deter_state] concatenated, shape (B, stoch+deter)

  • Process: MLP with configurable layers and hidden units

  • Output: Predicted quantity with distribution (normal, binary, or raw)

Supports three output types: - 'normal': Gaussian distribution for regression (rewards, values) - 'binary': Bernoulli distribution for binary classification (discount) - 'none': Raw tensor for non-probabilistic outputs

Usage:

reward_decoder = DenseDecoder(
    stoch_size=30,
    deter_size=200,
    output_shape=(1,),
    n_layers=2,
    units=400,
    activation='elu',
    dist='normal'
)
reward_dist = reward_decoder(latent_features)
reward_loss = -reward_dist.log_prob(target_reward)

For discount prediction (binary):

discount_decoder = DenseDecoder(
    stoch_size=30,
    deter_size=200,
    output_shape=(1,),
    n_layers=2,
    units=400,
    activation='elu',
    dist='binary'
)
Parameters:

decode_from_indices(indices, codebook)[source]#

Decode discrete token indices into images.

The codebook must be passed in explicitly – it is the quantizer’s table (IRISEncoder.quantizer.codebook), the only one the commitment and reconstruction losses train. This decoder previously owned a private index_to_embedding table that no objective ever touched, so decoding through it returned noise that looked plausible enough to go unnoticed.

simulusion.vision.vq_layer.restart_dead_codes(codebook, usage, z_flat, threshold)[source]#

Re-seed codebook entries that have fallen out of use.

Nearest-neighbour quantizers are prone to codebook collapse: a code that stops winning any assignment receives no further update and can never come back, so the effective vocabulary shrinks (visible as the perplexity metric dropping toward 1). The standard remedy is to periodically reset unused entries onto randomly drawn encoder outputs, which puts them back in a region of space where they can win assignments again.

Parameters:

  • codebook (Embedding) – The embedding table to modify in place.

  • usage (Tensor) – (vocab_size,) EMA of how often each code was selected. Under an EMA with decay d, this converges to the code’s mean assignments per step, so the threshold is interpretable in those units.

  • z_flat (Tensor) – (N, C) encoder outputs from the current batch, used as the pool of candidate re-seed locations.

  • threshold (float) – Codes with usage below this are considered dead. Values near 1.0 are far too aggressive for a full codebook – with V codes and roughly V assignments per step the mean usage is ~1, so half the book would be restarted every step. See DEFAULT_DEAD_CODE_THRESHOLD.

Returns:

(num_restarted, restarted_mask) – a scalar tensor counting the codes that were re-seeded, and the boolean mask identifying them. Callers that keep their own accumulators for the codebook (the EMA quantizer’s ema_embed_avg) need the mask: they cannot recover it afterwards by comparing usage against the threshold, because the restart deliberately lifts usage above it.

Return type:

tuple[Tensor, Tensor]

class simulusion.vision.video_tokenizer.VideoTokenizer(num_frames=16, image_size=64, in_channels=3, encoder_dim=512, decoder_dim=1024, encoder_depth=12, decoder_depth=20, num_heads=16, patch_size=4, vocab_size=1024, embedding_dim=32, commitment_weight=0.25, use_ema=False, ema_decay=0.99)[source]#

Bases: ExportableAgentMixin, Module

Video Tokenizer using VQ-VAE with Spatiotemporal Transformer.

This is a core component of Genie (Google DeepMind, 2024), used to compress raw video frames into discrete latent tokens that can be processed by downstream models like the LatentActionModel and DynamicsModel.

The tokenizer uses Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE) objective to learn a discrete codebook of video representations. Unlike standard VQ-VAE, this uses a Spatiotemporal (ST) Transformer in both encoder and decoder to better capture temporal dynamics in videos.

Architecture

  1. Patch Embedding: Convert (B, C, T, H, W) video to patch tokens

  2. Encoder ST-Transformer: Process spatial-temporal patches

  3. Vector Quantization: Discretize continuous embeddings to codebook entries

  4. Decoder ST-Transformer: Reconstruct video from quantized tokens

  5. Patch Unembedding: Convert tokens back to video frames

Key Features

  • Causal processing: Each frame’s encoding only uses previous frames

  • Discrete tokens: Enables autoregressive prediction with latent actions

  • Memory efficient: Uses ST-Transformer instead of full ViT to reduce complexity

Usage with Genie:

tokenizer = VideoTokenizer(
    num_frames=16,
    image_size=64,
    patch_size=4,
    vocab_size=1024,
    embedding_dim=32
)
reconstructed, indices, loss_dict = tokenizer(video_frames)

# For discrete token input to dynamics model:
token_embeddings = tokenizer.decode_indices(indices)

The tokenizer is trained with VQ-VAE objective: - Reconstruction loss: MSE between input and reconstructed video - VQ loss: Commit to codebook embeddings - Commitment loss: Penalizes encoder outputs drifting from codebook

Reference:

Genie: Generative Interactive Environments Bruce et al., Google DeepMind, 2024 - https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15391

class simulusion.blocks.st_transformer.STKVCache(num_layers, batch_size, num_heads, num_patches, head_dim, max_frames, device, dtype)[source]#

Bases: object

Per-layer temporal key/value cache for frame-by-frame generation.

In an ST-transformer, spatial attention and the MLP act within a frame and temporal attention is causal, so a frame’s activations never depend on later frames. Generating frame t+1 therefore only needs the temporal keys/values of frames 0..t - it does not have to re-run the network over the whole prefix. With the cache, each new frame costs one frame’s worth of compute instead of t frames’, turning an O(T^2) rollout into O(T).

Storage is a pre-allocated (B, heads, N, max_frames, head_dim) buffer per layer. Writes go to length onwards; advance() commits them. A forward that is not committed can be repeated (e.g. MaskGIT refinement of the same frame) and simply overwrites the same slots.

Parameters:

  • batch_size (int)

  • num_heads (int)

class simulusion.blocks.st_transformer.STSpatialAttention(dim, num_heads=8, qkv_bias=False, qk_scale=None, attn_drop=0.0, proj_drop=0.0)[source]#

Bases: Module

Spatial attention layer for spatiotemporal transformer.

Processes video tokens by attending over spatial positions (H*W) within each time step independently. Captures within-frame spatial relationships.

  • Input: (B, T, N, C) – B batches, T time steps, N spatial positions (H*W), C channels

  • Output: (B, T, N, C) – Same shape, spatially attended features

Architecture

  • QKV projection: Linear(dim, dim*3)

  • Reshape to multi-head attention format

  • Fused scaled dot-product attention (FlashAttention on supported GPUs)

  • Output projection

Applied to video tokens of shape (B, T, N, C) to capture within-frame spatial structure (e.g., object positions).

class simulusion.blocks.st_transformer.STTemporalAttention(dim, num_heads=8, qkv_bias=False, qk_scale=None, attn_drop=0.0, proj_drop=0.0)[source]#

Bases: Module

Temporal attention layer with causal masking for spatiotemporal transformer.

Processes video tokens by attending over time steps (T) across all spatial positions. Uses causal masking to ensure each frame only attends to previous frames (important for autoregressive video generation).

  • Input: (B, T, N, C) – B batches, T time steps, N spatial positions, C channels

  • Output: (B, T, N, C) – Same shape, temporally attended features

Causal masking

  • Frame t can only attend to frames 0…t-1

  • Prevents information leakage from future frames

  • Essential for autoregressive video generation models

Applied after STSpatialAttention to model temporal dynamics in the Genie VideoTokenizer.

Parameters:

  • dim (int)

  • num_heads (int)

  • qkv_bias (bool)

class simulusion.blocks.st_transformer.STTransformerBlock(dim, num_heads=8, mlp_ratio=4.0, qkv_bias=False, qk_scale=None, drop=0.0, attn_drop=0.0, drop_path=0.0, act_layer=<class 'torch.nn.modules.activation.GELU'>, norm_layer=<class 'torch.nn.modules.normalization.LayerNorm'>)[source]#

Bases: Module

Combined spatiotemporal transformer block with interleaved attention.

A single block applies:

  1. Spatial attention (within each time frame)

  2. Temporal attention (across frames with causal mask)

  3. MLP projection

The order is: x -> + SpatialAttn -> + TemporalAttn -> + MLP -> x

This interleaved design captures both spatial structure and temporal dynamics efficiently, used in Genie’s VideoTokenizer and DynamicsModel.

Parameters:

  • dim (int) – Feature dimension (must match patch embedding dimension)

  • num_heads (int) – Number of attention heads

  • mlp_ratio (float) – MLP hidden dim = dim * mlp_ratio

  • drop (float) – Dropout rates

  • attn_drop (float) – Dropout rates

  • drop_path (float) – Stochastic depth rate for drop path regularization

  • norm_layer (type[Module]) – Normalization layer class (default: nn.LayerNorm)

  • qkv_bias (bool)

  • qk_scale (float | None)

  • act_layer (type[Module])

Usage in Genie:

# VideoTokenizer encoder (12 layers)
encoder = STTransformer(
    num_frames=16,
    num_patches_per_frame=256,
    dim=512,
    depth=12,
    num_heads=16
)
encoded = encoder(tokens)  # (B, T*N, C)

# Dynamics model decoder (24 layers)
decoder = STTransformer(
    num_frames=16,
    num_patches_per_frame=256,
    dim=1024,
    depth=24,
    num_heads=16
)
decoded = decoder(tokens)

class simulusion.configs.JEPAConfig(use_bfloat16=False, model_name='vit_base', load_checkpoint=False, read_checkpoint=None, copy_data=False, pred_depth=None, pred_emb_dim=384, loss_type='l2', dataset='imagenet', val_split=None, use_gaussian_blur=False, use_horizontal_flip=False, use_color_distortion=False, color_jitter_strength=0.0, batch_size=2048, pin_mem=True, num_workers=8, root_path='/data/imagenet', image_folder='train', crop_size=224, crop_scale=(0.3, 1.0), download=False, allow_overlap=False, patch_size=16, num_enc_masks=1, min_keep=10, enc_mask_scale=(0.85, 1.0), num_pred_masks=4, pred_mask_scale=(0.15, 0.2), aspect_ratio=(0.75, 1.5), ema=(0.996, 1.0), ipe_scale=1.0, weight_decay=0.04, final_weight_decay=0.4, epochs=300, warmup=15, start_lr=0.0001, lr=0.001, final_lr=1e-06, lr_reference_batch_size=2048, early_stopping=False, patience=10, min_delta=0.0001, folder='results/jepa', write_tag='jepa_run', enable_wandb=False, wandb_project='simulusion', wandb_entity='', enable_sweep=False, sweep_config=<factory>)[source]

Bases: SerializableConfigMixin

Minimal configuration container for JEPA training. Converts to the nested dict expected by train_jepa.main.

Defaults reproduce I-JEPA as specified in the paper (Assran et al., CVPR 2023, Sec. 3 and Appendix A): no hand-crafted view augmentations, 4 target blocks of scale (0.15, 0.2), a single context block of scale (0.85, 1.0), and the paper’s AdamW/EMA schedules at the reference batch size of 2048. See configs/experiments/jepa_small_gpu.yaml for a single-GPU preset.

class simulusion.configs.DiTConfig(DATASET='CIFAR10', BATCH=256, EPOCHS=3, LR=0.0001, WEIGHT_DECAY=0.0, IMG_SIZE=32, CHANNELS=3, PATCH=4, WIDTH=384, DEPTH=12, HEADS=6, DROP=0.0, NUM_CLASSES=0, CLASS_DROPOUT_PROB=0.1, LEARN_SIGMA=True, BETA_START=0.0001, BETA_END=0.02, TIMESTEPS=1000, EMA=True, EMA_DECAY=0.9999, WORKDIR='./dit_demo', ROOT_PATH='./data', CHECKPOINT_EVERY=0, EARLY_STOPPING=False, PATIENCE=10, MIN_DELTA=0.0001, VAL_SPLIT=0.05, CROP_SIZE=None, NUM_WORKERS=4)[source]

Bases: SerializableConfigMixin

Default configuration values for Diffusion Transformer (DiT) training.

The fields define dataset selection, model architecture, diffusion schedule, optimization hyperparameters, and output paths used by the built-in training entrypoints.

Field names use UPPER_CASE for backward compatibility with the original DiT codebase. Snake-case aliases are accepted via __getattr__ and get_dit_config().

simulusion.configs.get_dit_config(**overrides)[source]

Returns a DiTConfig instance with default values overridden by the provided keyword arguments.

Both UPPER_CASE and snake_case override keys are accepted.

Example usage:

cfg = get_dit_config(BATCH=64, EPOCHS=10, LR=1e-3) cfg = get_dit_config(batch=64, epochs=10, lr=1e-3)

Parameters:

overrides (Any)

Return type:

DiTConfig

simulusion.configs.dit_preset_config(name, patch_size, **overrides)[source]

Build a config for a named Table 1 model, e.g. dit_preset_config("DiT-XL", 2).

Parameters:

  • name (str) – One of DiT-S, DiT-B, DiT-L, DiT-XL (case-insensitive, and the DiT- prefix is optional).

  • patch_size (int) – Latent patch size; the paper explores 2, 4 and 8.

  • **overrides (Any) – Further config fields, UPPER_CASE or snake_case.

Returns:

A DiTConfig for that model. Defaults target latent diffusion of 256x256 ImageNet: a 32x32x4 latent with 1000 classes.

Return type:

DiTConfig

  • scheduler_factor (float) – Multiplicative factor for learning rate reduction.

  • early_stopping_patience (int) – Epochs to wait before early stopping.

  • sample_interval (int) – Epoch interval for saving sample images.

class simulusion.configs.jepa_config.JEPAConfig(use_bfloat16=False, model_name='vit_base', load_checkpoint=False, read_checkpoint=None, copy_data=False, pred_depth=None, pred_emb_dim=384, loss_type='l2', dataset='imagenet', val_split=None, use_gaussian_blur=False, use_horizontal_flip=False, use_color_distortion=False, color_jitter_strength=0.0, batch_size=2048, pin_mem=True, num_workers=8, root_path='/data/imagenet', image_folder='train', crop_size=224, crop_scale=(0.3, 1.0), download=False, allow_overlap=False, patch_size=16, num_enc_masks=1, min_keep=10, enc_mask_scale=(0.85, 1.0), num_pred_masks=4, pred_mask_scale=(0.15, 0.2), aspect_ratio=(0.75, 1.5), ema=(0.996, 1.0), ipe_scale=1.0, weight_decay=0.04, final_weight_decay=0.4, epochs=300, warmup=15, start_lr=0.0001, lr=0.001, final_lr=1e-06, lr_reference_batch_size=2048, early_stopping=False, patience=10, min_delta=0.0001, folder='results/jepa', write_tag='jepa_run', enable_wandb=False, wandb_project='simulusion', wandb_entity='', enable_sweep=False, sweep_config=<factory>)[source]#

Bases: SerializableConfigMixin

Minimal configuration container for JEPA training. Converts to the nested dict expected by train_jepa.main.

Defaults reproduce I-JEPA as specified in the paper (Assran et al., CVPR 2023, Sec. 3 and Appendix A): no hand-crafted view augmentations, 4 target blocks of scale (0.15, 0.2), a single context block of scale (0.85, 1.0), and the paper’s AdamW/EMA schedules at the reference batch size of 2048. See configs/experiments/jepa_small_gpu.yaml for a single-GPU preset.

Training entry points#

Key classes and functions: DiamondAgent, train_diamond, train_dreamer, GenieTrainer, IRISTrainer, and related training entry points.

Training for every Simulusion family.

Trainer runs any TrainingTask (one or more per family, see simulusion.training.tasks) from a TrainerConfig; run() does it from a YAML run config. The per-family trainers below (IRISTrainer, train_diamond, …) are the older entrypoints, kept for existing scripts.

Complete World Model training pipeline for any Gym environment.

This script trains a complete World Model pipeline consisting of: 1. ConvVAE - Encodes observations into latent space 2. MDNRNN - Predicts future latent states given actions 3. Controller - Linear controller trained with CMA-ES

Usage:

python train_world_model.py –env CarRacing-v3 –data_dir ./data –logdir ./results python train_world_model.py –env BipedalWalker-v3 –action_size 4 # if env loading fails

The script will: 1. Generate rollout data (if not already present) 2. Train VAE 3. Train MDNRNN 4. Train Controller

Training script for Convolutional Variational Autoencoder (ConvVAE).

This module provides functions to train a ConvVAE model on observation data for world model learning.

simulusion.training.train_convvae.train_convae(config)[source]#

Train a Convolutional VAE model.

Runs on the shared Trainer through the vae task, on the rollouts in config.data_dir (.npz files with observations, or any episode folder). As before, everything goes to <logdir>/vae:

  • checkpoint.tar every epoch and best.tar for the lowest held-out loss (the last 600 rollouts are held out when there are more), resumed from unless noreload is set

  • ReduceLROnPlateau and early stopping on that loss

  • samples/sample_epoch_<N>.png every sample_interval epochs unless nosamples

  • convae_final.pth, the final weights

The trainer adds checkpoints/, run.json, run_config.yaml and train_metrics.jsonl.

Example

>>> config = WMVAEConfig(
...     height=64, width=64, latent_size=32, num_epochs=100, logdir='results'
... )
>>> train_convae(config)
Parameters:

config (WMVAEConfig)

Return type:

None

Training script for Mixture Density Recurrent Neural Network (MDRNN).

This module provides functions to train an MDRNN model for sequence prediction in world models. The MDRNN predicts future latent states using a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) based on current latent states and actions.

simulusion.training.train_mdn_rnn.get_loss(mdrnn, latent_obs, action, reward, terminal, latent_next_obs, include_reward, latent_size)[source]#

Compute MDRNN loss.

Computes the combined loss for the MDRNN model: - GMM loss for next latent state prediction - BCE loss for terminal state prediction - MSE loss for reward prediction (if include_reward is True)

Parameters:

  • mdrnn (MDRNN) – MDRNN model.

  • latent_obs (Tensor) – Current latent observations.

  • action (Tensor) – Actions taken.

  • reward (Tensor) – Rewards received.

  • terminal (Tensor) – Terminal state flags.

  • latent_next_obs (Tensor) – Next latent observations (target).

  • include_reward (bool) – Whether to include reward prediction in loss.

  • latent_size (int) – Size of latent space.

Returns:

Dictionary containing gmm, bce, mse, and total loss values.

Return type:

dict[str, Tensor]

simulusion.training.train_mdn_rnn.train_mdn_rnn(vae_config, mdrnn_config, use_precomputed_latents=True, use_amp=True)[source]#

Train an MDRNN model.

Runs on the shared Trainer through the mdrnn task, on the rollouts in mdrnn_config.data_dir, encoded by the VAE in <vae_config.logdir>/vae/best.tar. As before, everything goes to <mdrnn_config.logdir>/mdrnn: checkpoint.tar every epoch, best.tar for the lowest held-out loss (resumed from unless noreload), ReduceLROnPlateau and early stopping on that loss, and mdrnn_final.pth.

Parameters:

  • vae_config (WMVAEConfig) – WMVAEConfig for loading pretrained VAE.

  • mdrnn_config (WMMDNRNNConfig) – WMMDNRNNConfig with the MDN-RNN’s settings.

  • use_precomputed_latents (bool) – Accepted for compatibility. Latents are sampled from the VAE as each batch is drawn, so every epoch sees fresh samples instead of one fixed draw stored on disk.

  • use_amp (bool) – fp16 with loss scaling, on CUDA.

Return type:

None

Example

>>> vae_config = WMVAEConfig(
...     height=64, width=64, latent_size=32, logdir='results'
... )
>>> mdrnn_config = WMMDNRNNConfig(
...     latent_size=32, action_size=3, hidden_size=256,
...     gmm_components=5, logdir='results'
... )
>>> train_mdn_rnn(vae_config, mdrnn_config)

Training a linear controller on latent + recurrent state with CMA-ES.

This module provides functions to train a linear controller using Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES). The controller maps latent and hidden states to actions for the learned world model.

Reference:

Ha & Schmidhuber (2018). Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution. https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.11111

simulusion.training.train_controller.make_controller_env(env_name)[source]#

env_name as the controller sees it: 64x64 image observations.

Environments that take continuous (CarRacing) get the continuous action space the World Models controller outputs. Environments are made with render_mode="rgb_array", so those whose observations are vectors (Pendulum, BipedalWalker) are seen through their rendered frames.

Parameters:

env_name (str)

Return type:

Any

simulusion.training.train_controller.train_controller(config)[source]#

Train a linear controller using CMA-ES.

Runs on the shared Trainer through the controller task, with the VAE and MDN-RNN in <logdir>/vae/best.tar and <logdir>/mdrnn/best.tar. One step is one CMA-ES generation of pop_size candidates, each scored over n_samples episodes of up to time_limit steps in env_name. The best controller so far is kept in <logdir>/ctrl/best.tar (and started from when it exists); training stops when CMA-ES converges or the best return passes target_return.

Candidates are scored one after another in this process, so max_workers and display no longer apply. The controller’s sizes come from the trained models, whatever latent_size / hidden_size / action_size say.

Parameters:

config (WMControllerConfig) – WMControllerConfig containing training hyperparameters, including env_name and action_size.

Return type:

None

simulusion.training.train_jepa.build_loss_fn(loss_type)[source]#

Return the prediction loss used to compare predictor and target tokens.

The I-JEPA paper (Sec. 3) defines the objective as the squared L2 distance between predicted and target patch representations, averaged over the M target blocks. Two reductions of that same objective are offered:

  • "l2" (default) averages the squared error over patches and channels as well. It has the same minimizer and the same gradient direction as the paper’s formula, but a magnitude that does not grow with block size – which is what the paper’s learning rates were tuned against, since the reference implementation also reduces by mean.

  • "l2_sum" is the literal formula: summed over patches within a block, averaged over blocks. Its gradients are larger than "l2"’s by roughly the number of patches times the embedding dimension, so lower the learning rate accordingly.

"smooth_l1" reproduces the reference implementation, which uses Smooth-L1 rather than the paper’s L2.

Parameters:

loss_type (str)

Return type:

Any

preprocess_frame(frame)[source]#

Preprocess frame: resize to 64x64, return CHW uint8.

Frames are kept as uint8 because that is the dtype of the replay buffer (IRISReplayBuffer.observations). Returning floats in [0, 1] here silently truncated every pixel to 0 on insertion, so the world model and policy trained exclusively on black images. Normalisation to [0, 1] happens at consumption time via to_float_tensor().

Parameters:

frame (ndarray)

Return type:

ndarray

Return type:

collect_experience(num_steps, epsilon=0.01)[source]#

Collect exactly num_steps environment steps (paper Algorithm 1).

The step count is exact because the Atari 100k budget is defined in environment steps: collection_epochs * env_steps_per_epoch must equal 100k. Episodes span epochs, so the environment, the policy’s LSTM state and the running episode return all persist between calls and are reset only on a real episode boundary.

Two details follow the paper rather than convenience:

  • Frames are passed through the discrete autoencoder before reaching the policy (A.1), because the policy is trained purely on reconstructions.

  • The LSTM state is threaded across steps (A.3); the policy is recurrent and a per-step reset would leave it unable to perceive motion.

Parameters:

  • num_steps (int) – Exact number of environment steps to collect

  • epsilon (float) – Random action probability

Returns:

Mean return of episodes that finished during this call, or the most recently completed episode’s return if none finished.

Return type:

float

epoch (int) – Current epoch number

Returns:

Return type:

dict

get_epsilon(epoch)[source]#

Exploration epsilon for collection.

Paper Table 5 uses a fixed epsilon-greedy parameter of 0.01 combined with sampling from the policy, rather than the decaying schedule most Atari 100k baselines use (Appendix H discusses the tradeoff). A decaying schedule starting near-random makes the early world model fit a data distribution the policy never revisits.

Parameters:

epoch (int)

Return type:

float

class simulusion.memory.dreamer_memory.ReplayBuffer(size, obs_shape, action_size, seq_len, batch_size)[source]#

Bases: object

Fixed-size replay buffer for Dreamer with image observations and transitions.

Stores (observation, action, reward, terminal) tuples in a ring buffer and supports sampling contiguous sequences for world-model training.

Key Features

  • Ring buffer with fixed capacity (FIFO eviction when full)

  • Stores raw uint8 images to save memory

  • Samples sequences (not single transitions) for temporal modeling

  • Validates sampled sequences don’t span episode boundaries

Memory Layout

  • observations: (capacity, C, H, W) uint8 images

  • actions: (capacity, action_dim) float32

  • rewards: (capacity,) float32

  • terminals: (capacity,) float32 (1.0 = terminal, 0.0 = continue)

Sampling Process

  1. Random start index (avoiding episode boundaries)

  2. Collect sequence of length seq_len with wraparound

  3. Validate no terminal in middle of sequence

  4. Return batch of sequences

Usage with Dreamer:

buffer = ReplayBuffer(
    size=100000,           # Max transitions to store
    obs_shape=(3, 64, 64), # RGB images
    action_size=6,         # Continuous action dim
    seq_len=50,            # Sequence length for training
    batch_size=50          # Parallel sequences per batch
)

# Add transitions during interaction
buffer.add(obs, action, reward, done)

# Sample batch for world model training
obs_batch, action_batch, reward_batch, term_batch = buffer.sample()

Memory Efficiency

  • Uses uint8 for images (1 byte per pixel vs 4 for float32)

  • Sequences share observations (overlapping windows)

  • Configurable capacity based on available system memory

Note

The buffer stores observations as {“image”: …} dicts but returns just the image arrays for training efficiency.

Parameters:

  • size (int)

  • obs_shape (Tuple[int, ...])

  • action_size (int)

  • seq_len (int)

  • batch_size (int)

add(obs, ac, rew, done, terminated=None)[source]#

Add a transition to the buffer.

Parameters:

  • obs (dict) – Observation dict with ‘image’ key containing the observation

  • ac (ndarray) – Action taken, shape (action_size,)

  • rew (float) – Reward received, scalar

  • done (float) – Episode-boundary flag, 1.0 if the episode ended for any reason (termination or truncation), 0.0 otherwise

  • terminated (float | None) – 1.0 only if the environment genuinely terminated. Defaults to done when the caller cannot tell the two apart.

Return type:

None

Episode-based replay memory for PlaNet/RSSM training.

Stores episodes as variable-length trajectories and supports sampling sub-sequences for training. Implements a ring-buffer style eviction when capacity is reached.

  • Supports time-major formatting (time-first) for RNN input

memory = Memory(size=100)
memory.append([episode1, episode2])

sample_with_burn_in(batch_size, burn_in)[source]#

Sample start frames together with the frames that precede them.

IRIS burns in the previous frames to initialise the actor-critic’s LSTM state before imagining from a given frame (paper A.3). This returns both halves so the caller does not have to reason about buffer indexing.

Episode boundaries are respected: any burn-in frame at or before a terminal is replaced by a repeat of the oldest valid frame, so context never bleeds across episodes.

Parameters:

  • batch_size (int) – Number of start frames to draw.

  • burn_in (int) – Number of preceding frames to return per start frame.

Returns:

(batch_size, C, H, W) uint8 frames to imagine from. burn_in_obs: (batch_size, burn_in, C, H, W) uint8 preceding frames.

Empty along axis 1 when burn_in is 0.

Return type:

start_obs
